answer: Document the eleven-day trial itself as an E16 Measurement, not an E14 Condition Assessment. What the observatory actually did -- running the chronometer against its own regulator clock and noting the accumulated gain or loss at noon each day -- is exactly E16's 'systematic, objective procedure of direct observation' of a physical thing, and it terminates in a quantifiable value (the daily rate, in seconds gained or lost per day) rather than a qualitative preservation state. Model it as: the trial (E16) P39 measured the chronometer (E18); P40 observed dimension an E54 Dimension for the daily rate (P90 has value / P91 has unit, e.g. seconds per day); P14 carried out by the observatory; P4 has time-span the eleven days. E14 Condition Assessment is the wrong fit for the trial itself: its required properties are P34 concerned (E18) and P35 has identified an E3 Condition State, and every worked example of E3 in the corpus (t1406, Issue 672) is a qualitative preservation/damage state identified by inspection -- 'broken', 'fine', 'wrecked', 'cockled' -- reached by looking at the object, not by comparing it against a reference instrument over days. Nothing in the case describes the observatory inspecting the chronometer's physical condition. The certificate's second statement -- 'fit for sea service' -- is a judgement drawn from the measured rate, not a separate inspection either, so it is best modelled as a further E17 Type Assignment (classifying the chronometer as of type 'fit for sea service', P17 was motivated by the E16 Measurement) rather than as reason to reclassify the trial as E14. E17's own scope note fits this: it is for classifications 'in cases where the value of the classification depends on the personal opinion of the classifier' -- which is exactly what turning a measured rate into a seaworthiness verdict is. The certificate itself is an E31 Document that P70 documents both the E16 Measurement and, if modelled, the E17 Type Assignment.

rejected_alternatives.why_not: E14's required properties point to P34 concerned (E18) and P35 has identified an E3 Condition State; the corpus's own worked E3 examples (t1406, Issue 672) are qualitative preservation/damage states reached by inspection ('broken', 'fine', 'wrecked', 'cockled'), not a numeric rate reached by comparison against a reference clock over eleven days. The case gives no inspection of physical condition, only a running comparison against the regulator clock.

rejected_alternatives.option: Folding the fitness declaration into the same E16 Measurement
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E16's scope note ties the class to determining a value by direct observation of physical reality; 'fit for sea service' is not itself an observed physical quantity but a judgement drawn from one, matching E17 Type Assignment's scope note about classifications that depend on the classifier's opinion rather than E16's objective procedure.
